Chapter 2: The Roots of Forgiveness — Amish Faith and Everyday Life
If you really want to understand how the Amish could respond to such a heartbreaking tragedy with forgiveness, you’ve got to step into their world for a while. Not just for a day, but through those quiet, everyday routines that shape who they are.
For the Amish, faith isn’t just a list of beliefs or something they practice on Sundays. It’s in every detail of daily life. The way they dress, how they work, the way they raise their children, and even how they interact with neighbors—it all springs from their deep-rooted faith.
Picture an Amish home before sunrise. The day starts early, with everyone sharing chores. Meals are simple, and there’s a sense of calm, with no TVs or computers, and definitely no cars parked out front. Instead, their days are built around a steady rhythm of work, worship, and community.
Kids learn pretty early that what they do reflects on their family and their church. Humility is something they really value, and pride? That’s gently set aside.
At the center of Amish faith is the teaching of Jesus—especially his call to forgive, just as God forgives. This isn’t just a Sunday lesson; it’s a principle for everyday living. So, whenever someone in the community is hurt—whether it’s a harsh word, a broken promise, or something much more serious—there’s a clear expectation: forgiveness isn’t optional; it’s essential.
Why? Because forgiveness keeps the community whole. It stops bitterness from spreading and breaking those vital bonds.
This idea is reinforced by something called “Meidung,” or shunning. When someone breaks the rules of the church and won’t admit it, they’re gently, but firmly, excluded from meals and social gatherings. But here’s the key: the goal isn’t to punish—it’s to restore. If the person comes back and asks for forgiveness, the community welcomes them with open arms.
It’s a living example that, no matter the offense, forgiveness is always possible.
For most Amish folks, forgiving isn’t about some big dramatic moment. It’s a quiet choice—made again and again. It’s a habit, built up over years and supported by those around them. When someone’s hurt, they’re encouraged to let go of anger and look for peace. That doesn’t mean ignoring the pain or forgetting about justice. Instead, forgiveness is a way to release the heavy weight of resentment, and trust that God will put things right in the end.
Their view of forgiveness is also shaped by how they see suffering. Life, for the Amish, is full of challenges and loss. But rather than seeing this as a sign that God’s abandoned them, they see it as a chance to grow in faith and compassion. When tragedy happens, the whole community comes together—sharing chores, bringing meals, and lifting each other up in prayer. Suffering, in this way, becomes something shared. And forgiveness becomes a shared practice, too.
After the Nickel Mines shooting, it became clear that the Amish way of forgiveness isn’t about forgetting the pain or excusing what happened. It’s about making a conscious choice—a choice to value healing over revenge, and community over isolation.
Most of us don’t realize just how much strength it takes to forgive, especially when the wounds are still fresh. But for the Amish, that strength doesn’t come from themselves alone. It’s rooted in a deep trust in God, and a belief that grace is always possible—even when things feel darkest.
